title: Silk Route permits and rules: who, where and how
meta_description: How the Old Silk Route permit works in 2026: Indians only, processed at Rongli, about ₹200, documents, check posts, vehicle rules and the Kupup crossing.
summary: The Old Silk Route beyond Rongli is a protected area open to Indian nationals only. Your driver, agent or homestay processes the permit at Rongli for about ₹200 per person plus handling, with a photo ID and two photos. Foreigners cannot go to Zuluk, Nathang or Kupup. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Why the Silk Route needs a permit
paras: The road from Rongli up through Lingtam, Padamchen and Zuluk to Nathang and Kupup runs close to the border with the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. Jelep La, the old trade pass, is a few kilometres from Kupup, and the Doklam plateau can be seen from the ridges above Nathang. The Army has camps along the whole road, and Zuluk itself grew around an Army transit camp. For these reasons the area beyond Rongli is a protected area, and every visitor needs a permit issued in their name for specific dates and a specific vehicle.

None of this makes the trip difficult. Thousands of Indian families do it every season, and the paperwork is handled by the people you are already paying: your driver, your agent or your first homestay. What matters is that you carry the right documents, start early enough, and do not assume rules from an old blog still apply. Everything below is the rule as we understand it in October 2026. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Who can go, and who cannot
paras: The Silk Route is open to Indian nationals only. Foreign nationals, including holders of an OCI card, are not allowed to Zuluk, Nathang, Kupup or the other places beyond Rongli, even with a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. This is one of the clearest rules in Sikkim and it is checked at the posts.

If you are travelling with a foreign partner or friend, they can still enjoy a lot of Pakyong district. Aritar, Lampokhari Lake, Rhenock and Pakyong town lie outside the protected area and only need the general Sikkim entry permit that every foreigner gets online. From Gangtok, foreigners in a group of two or more can visit Tsomgo Lake on a one-day permit. Plan the Silk Route for the Indian members of the group on a separate day, or choose a route that suits everyone.
list: Indian nationals: allowed with a Silk Route permit
Foreign nationals and OCI holders: not allowed beyond Rongli
Aritar, Rhenock, Pakyong town: no protected-area permit needed (Rolep: ask us)
Tsomgo Lake from Gangtok: separate permit, Indians and foreigners (foreigners in groups of 2 or more)
Nathu La: separate permit, Indians only, usually Wednesday to Sunday

sections.heading: Documents and fees
paras: Each traveller needs an original government photo ID and two recent passport-size photographs. Aadhaar, a voter card, a passport or a driving licence are the usual choices; carry the original and a photocopy, because some posts keep a copy. Children carry a school ID or birth certificate along with an Aadhaar card if they have one. Send the scans to whoever is processing the permit a day or two before you arrive, and keep the originals in a pocket, not in the car boot.

The government fee is about ₹200 per person. Agents and homestays usually charge between ₹300 and ₹700 per person including the processing, the trip to the office and the vehicle paperwork. That is fair: someone has to stand in the queue at Rongli. Ask whether the permit fee is inside your package price.

sections.heading: How the Rongli permit actually works
paras: Most travellers arriving from NJP, Bagdogra or Gangtok reach Rongli between late morning and early afternoon. Your driver takes your documents into the office, the permit is prepared for your names, dates and vehicle number, and you continue up the hill. On a good day this takes 30 to 60 minutes. On a busy October Saturday it can take two hours, which is one reason we suggest a first night at Padamchen or Lingtam rather than pushing to Nathang.

Many homestays at Zuluk and Padamchen now arrange the permit in advance from your scanned documents, so the paper is waiting at Rongli. This is the easiest way. Offices keep government hours, close on some holidays and sometimes stop issuing after mid-afternoon. If you arrive late, you may have to sleep at Rongli, Lingtam or Rolep and go up the next morning.
You will show the permit at check posts along the road. Keep it with your ID until you are back below Rongli or over Kupup towards Gangtok.

sections.heading: Vehicles, timings and the Kupup crossing
paras: The permit names the vehicle as well as the people. Sikkim-registered tourist taxis are the standard choice and the drivers know every post. Cars registered outside Sikkim, including West Bengal taxis and private cars, have faced restrictions on this road at different times, so do not plan a self-drive trip without asking us first. Bikers usually need extra paperwork; again, ask.

The high road continues from Nathang past Old Baba Mandir and Kupup to the Gangtok–Nathu La road near Sherathang and Tsomgo Lake. Some trips cross this way between Gangtok and the Silk Route in one day, which saves the long return to Rongli. It needs a Tsomgo-side permit from Gangtok as well as the Silk Route permit, a driver whose vehicle is on both, and clearance from the posts on that day. It is not always allowed, it shuts after heavy snow, and the rules have changed more than once. Treat it as possible but not guaranteed, keep the Rongli road as your fall-back, and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Rules on the road
paras: The Silk Route passes through Army areas, and a few simple rules keep everyone out of trouble. Drivers will remind you, but it helps to know them in advance.
list: Do not photograph Army camps, bunkers, vehicles, check posts or soldiers. Ask your driver where photography is fine.
Stay on the road and marked viewpoints. Do not wander off towards the ridges near Kupup or Jelep La.
Do not fly drones anywhere on the route.
Carry your permit and ID at all times, including on short walks from Zuluk or Nathang.
Take your rubbish back down. Homestays burn or carry out what they can, and plastic left at Thambi stays there.
Do not pick rhododendron flowers or disturb yaks and their herders around Nathang and Kupup.

sections.heading: Common permit mistakes
paras: We see the same few problems every season. A traveller sends a blurred Aadhaar scan and the permit cannot be prepared. A group arrives at Rongli at four in the afternoon on a holiday. Someone forgets that their friend is a foreign national, or that their cousin's OCI card does not count as Indian citizenship for this purpose. A family adds a night at the last minute and the dates on the permit no longer match. Each of these is easy to avoid if you send clear documents two days ahead, reach Rongli by early afternoon, and tell us about any change before the trip, not at the check post.

One more point: keep a few photocopies of each ID and two spare photos in the car. Posts sometimes ask for a copy, and a second permit for Tsomgo or Nathu La needs the same documents again in Gangtok.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for Zuluk and the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Yes. All Indian visitors need a protected-area permit for the Old Silk Route beyond Rongli, covering places such as Padamchen, Zuluk, Thambi, Nathang and Kupup. It is processed at Rongli through a registered agent, driver or homestay for about ₹200 per person plus handling. You need a photo ID and two passport photos. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Zuluk or the Old Silk Route?
faqs.a: No. Foreign nationals, including OCI card holders, are not allowed to Zuluk, Nathang, Kupup or other places beyond Rongli, even with a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. They can visit Aritar, Lampokhari, Rhenock and Pakyong town in Pakyong district, and Tsomgo Lake from Gangtok in a group of two or more. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do I get the Silk Route permit?
faqs.a: The permit is processed at Rongli, the market town at the foot of the route, through a registered tour agent, your driver or your homestay. Many homestays prepare it in advance from scanned documents so it is ready when you arrive. You cannot simply walk up to a check post and get one on the spot. Allow 30 minutes to 2 hours at Rongli.

faqs.q: What documents are needed for the Silk Route permit?
faqs.a: Each traveller needs an original government photo ID, such as Aadhaar, a voter card, passport or driving licence, plus two recent passport-size photos. Carry a photocopy of the ID as well. Children need a school ID, birth certificate or Aadhaar. The vehicle details are added by the driver. Send clear scans a day or two ahead to whoever processes the permit.

faqs.q: How long does the Rongli permit take?
faqs.a: Usually 30 to 60 minutes on a normal day, and up to 2 hours on busy weekends in October, April and May. If your homestay or agent has prepared it in advance from scanned documents, it can be a quick stop. Offices keep government hours and may stop issuing by mid-afternoon, so aim to reach Rongli by early afternoon.

faqs.q: Can I drive my own car on the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Possibly, but do not count on it. The permit names the vehicle, and cars registered outside Sikkim, including private cars and West Bengal taxis, have faced restrictions on this road at different times. Sikkim-registered tourist taxis are the standard choice. Ask us about the current rule before planning a self-drive trip, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I go from Gangtok to Zuluk via Tsomgo and Kupup?
faqs.a: Sometimes. The high road links Nathang and Kupup with the Gangtok–Nathu La road near Tsomgo Lake, and some trips cross it in one day. You need both a Tsomgo permit from Gangtok and the Silk Route permit, a vehicle on both, and clearance on the day. It closes after heavy snow and the rules change, so keep the Rongli road as a fall-back.

faqs.q: Do children need a permit for the Silk Route?
faqs.a: Yes, every traveller is named on the permit, children included, so carry a school ID, birth certificate or Aadhaar for each child. Children under 5 are exempt from the ₹50 Sikkim entry fee. For very young children we suggest sleeping at Padamchen or Zuluk rather than Nathang, which is about 4,000 m. Ask us about current rules for infants.

faqs.q: Is a drone allowed on the Silk Route?
faqs.a: No. Do not fly a drone anywhere on the Old Silk Route. The road runs through Army areas close to the international border, and drones can be confiscated and lead to serious trouble. Photography of Army camps, vehicles, bunkers and check posts is also not allowed. Landscapes, villages with permission and viewpoints such as Thambi are fine.
